clue.text: Gravelly area in bay?

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another means it is placed inside it

blocks.note: a bay is a reddish-brown horse
A is the standard abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A crossword-style question: is there some stony patch out in the bay?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bay' looks like a stretch of coast; it is a horse's colour, used for the horse itself. HORSE takes A inside to give HOARSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A gravelly voice is rough and husky, which is exactly what a hoarse voice sounds like.

clue.text: Spooner's vastly superior crackers

indicators.note: Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words, so this signals that swap

blocks.note: vastly superior is way higher; swap the opening sounds of the two words

explanation.surface: Someone boasts that their Christmas crackers are vastly better than anyone else's.
explanation.walkthrough: WAY HIGHER with its first sounds swapped becomes HAY WIRE, written as one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal words for mad or out of control: a person gone haywire has gone crackers.

clue.text: Current Head of Accounts loves paper clips

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept
a clip holds something in its grip, so the paper wraps around what follows

blocks.note: the opening letter of Accounts
FT is the Financial Times, a newspaper
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O; two of them

explanation.surface: The present head of the accounts department is fond of paper clips.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' reads as an adjective for the department head; it is the definition. A then FT holding OO gives AFOOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something afoot is under way or in progress, which is what current means of a plan or event.

clue.text: Aspiring actress beginning to grasp essential elements of talent

indicators.note: to grasp something is to hold it tightly within, so one piece goes inside the other
the essential part of a word is its core, so only the middle letters are kept

blocks.note: a beginning is a start
the two central letters of talent

explanation.surface: A hopeful young actress is starting to understand what real talent consists of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beginning to grasp' reads as one phrase meaning starting to understand; split it, so the first word supplies a synonym and the rest tells it to hold something.
explanation.definitionFit: A starlet is a young actress hoping to become a star, so she is an aspiring one.

clue.text: Much was right, leaders conceded

indicators.note: the leaders of the words are given up, so each word loses its first letter

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Election night: the right-wing parties did well, and their leaders admitted defeat.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping the first letters of WAS and RIGHT leaves AS and IGHT, which read as A SIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: In informal British speech, 'a sight better' means much better, so the phrase works as an intensifying adverb.

clue.text: Traps extremely sportive sheep

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only its outermost letters are kept

blocks.note: the first and last letters of sportive
tups are rams, male sheep

explanation.surface: A wry remark that very playful sheep are a snare for the unwary.
explanation.walkthrough: A tup is a ram, a farming word common in northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: A set-up is a trap or frame arranged to catch someone, so set-ups are traps.

clue.text: Ale during broadcast of part of speech

indicators.note: seed that is broadcast is scattered widely, so these letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A beer drunk while part of a speech is going out on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'During' looks like a link between ale and the broadcast, but it is all fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Gerundial is the adjective from gerund, a verb form used as a noun, which is one part of speech.

clue.text: Harry Potter inhaling drug in plane, perhaps at height

indicators.note: to harry is to harass and stir up, so the letters of the next word are churned
breathing something in takes it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: taken as written
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: The boy wizard takes drugs on an aeroplane, presumably while flying high.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry Potter' reads as the boy wizard; Harry is the anagram signal. 'Plane' is not an aircraft but the plane tree.
explanation.definitionFit: A plane is a kind of tree, so the height of a plane is its crown, the treetop.

clue.text: Hypothetical computer resolved haunting crime

indicators.note: a crime that is resolved has been worked out and put in order, so these letters are reworked

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A theoretical computer has cracked a crime that had long haunted investigators.
explanation.walkthrough: Alan Turing's codebreaking makes a computer solving a crime a fitting picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Turing's abstract machine is a mathematical model of computation, never built, so it is a theoretical computer.

clue.text: Apprentice in utility room

indicators.note: the answer lies in the following words, running across them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A trainee is put to work in the room with the washing machine.
explanation.definitionFit: A tyro is a beginner or novice, just as an apprentice is someone still learning a trade.

clue.text: Cheating wanton finally repented at leisure

definitions.note: the answer is a plural noun; the gerund names the activity

indicators.note: wanton means unruly and undisciplined, so these letters run wild into a new order
finally points to the closing letter only of the word that follows

blocks.note: the closing letter of repented
taken as written

explanation.surface: Echoes the proverb 'marry in haste, repent at leisure', here about a faithless spouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wanton' fits the surface as a word for the cheater, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Adulteries are acts of marital infidelity, the cheating of one partner on another.

clue.text: Sherlock nicked sawn-off weapon

indicators.note: something sawn off has had its end cut away, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: Sherlock Holmes is a private investigator, a PI
nicked is British slang for stole

explanation.surface: The great detective has pinched a sawn-off shotgun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sawn-off' looks like it describes the weapon; it cuts the last letter from STOLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A pistol is a small handgun, one kind of weapon.

clue.text: Solidarity among rogues escaping justice

definitions.note: a phrase describing the state the noun names

blocks.note: an imp is a rascal or rogue; the plural serves the surface
solidarity is unity of purpose

explanation.surface: Honour among thieves: villains sticking together so that none of them is caught.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Among' places the two pieces together here rather than one inside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Impunity is exemption from punishment, the condition of someone who gets away without facing the law.

clue.text: Background checks lead to mortifying retreat

indicators.note: to check something is to hold it back, so one piece is held inside the other
the lead of a word is its front, so only its opening letter is kept

blocks.note: your heritage is your background or inherited tradition
the opening letter of mortifying

explanation.surface: A vetting check turns up something so embarrassing that the candidate withdraws.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Background checks' reads as vetting, but the phrase splits: HERITAGE holds M.
explanation.definitionFit: A hermitage is a secluded dwelling where a hermit lives apart, a place of retreat.

clue.text: Workers work with American and enjoy the change

blocks.note: men as in workmen, a workforce
OP is short for opus, a work
A is a standard abbreviation for American
to enjoy something is to have the use of it, as in enjoying a right

explanation.surface: Workers get on with an American colleague and welcome a shake-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The change' looks like a reorganisation at work; it is a euphemism. 'Enjoy' in the sense of having the use of something, as one enjoys a privilege.
explanation.definitionFit: The change, or change of life, is a long-standing euphemism for the end of a woman's menstruation.

clue.text: Doctor accepts one's a fetishist

indicators.note: accepting something takes it in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a GP is a general practitioner, a family doctor
one's is read as one is, which in the first person is I'm

explanation.surface: A doctor agrees that a patient has a fetish.
explanation.walkthrough: GP is the British name for a family doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: In slang a gimp is a person dressed in a bondage suit for sexual role-play, so a kind of fetishist.

clue.text: Sanctimony about holy books

blocks.note: CA is circa, Latin for about
NT is the New Testament

explanation.surface: Pious hypocrisy concerning scripture.
explanation.definitionFit: Cant is hypocritical, sanctimonious talk, especially of a moralising or religious kind.

clue.text: Roman's first day in California draws to a close

blocks.note: Cal is a short form of California
something that draws to a close ends

explanation.surface: An Italian's opening day on a West Coast trip comes to an end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roman's' looks like any Italian; it means the ancient Roman calendar.
explanation.definitionFit: In the ancient Roman calendar the calends was the first day of each month.

clue.text: Wasted talent is a torment

indicators.note: something wasted is ruined and thrown about, so these letters lose their order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Seeing ability go to waste is agony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' plays two parts: the second 'is' belongs to the fodder, while the clue's grammar uses it as a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To tantalise is to torment by keeping something desired just out of reach, as Tantalus was.

clue.text: Overwhelmed by strain, queen hides here

indicators.note: something overwhelmed is engulfed, so it ends up inside the other piece

blocks.note: to strain is to try hard, to make an effort
Anne was a queen of Great Britain

explanation.surface: A queen, overcome by stress, conceals herself in this place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hides' reads as a verb for the queen; it is the noun, animal skins.
explanation.definitionFit: A tannery is the works where animal skins are turned into leather, so that is where hides are.

clue.text: Wrongdoing of rising stable worker under scrutiny

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means the word reads upwards from bottom to top

blocks.note: to scan is to scrutinise, and what is under scrutiny is being scanned
a stable lad is a groom who looks after racehorses

explanation.surface: An up-and-coming stable hand is being investigated for misconduct.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer the second piece sits under the first, which the clue's 'under' also suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: A scandal is disgraceful conduct that causes public outrage, which is a form of wrongdoing.

clue.text: Ravel knocking back the Spanish fly

indicators.note: knocking something back sends it the other way, so the words are read in reverse

blocks.note: el is Spanish for the
a gnat is a small fly

explanation.surface: The composer Ravel downing the Spanish fly, an alleged aphrodisiac.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ravel' tempts as the French composer; it is a verb. Spanish fly is a notorious supposed aphrodisiac.
explanation.definitionFit: To ravel is to entangle or snarl threads, so it shares a meaning with tangle.

clue.text: Shambolic friends making comeback with panache

indicators.note: a comeback is a return, so the word travels back the way it came

blocks.note: pals are friends
dash is style and flair, like panache

explanation.surface: Disorganised friends return to the stage with flamboyant style.
explanation.definitionFit: Slapdash means careless and hurried, so the work it describes is a shambles.

clue.text: Reportedly drank case of amber liquid

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by voice, so the word is taken by its sound
a case is the outer shell, so only the outside letters of the word are kept

blocks.note: to neck a drink is British slang for gulping it down
the first and last letters of amber

explanation.surface: Someone apparently downed a whole crate of amber beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' suggests a crate of beer; it takes the shell of amber.
explanation.definitionFit: Nectar is the sweet liquid in flowers, and also the drink of the gods.

clue.text: Slice of exotic rum baba for Whit

indicators.note: a slice is a piece cut out of something larger, so the answer is cut from the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of exotic through rum into baba

explanation.surface: A piece of a fancy rum-soaked cake served at Whitsun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whit' looks like Whitsun, the Christian festival; it is a tiny amount.
explanation.definitionFit: A whit is the smallest particle of something, as is a crumb, as in 'not a crumb of comfort'.

clue.text: Cryptic clue ending in gratification

indicators.note: cryptic means obscured or puzzling, so the letters are disguised in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A solver's satisfaction at reaching the last clue of a cryptic puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Indulgence is the satisfying of a desire or pleasure, which is gratification.

clue.text: Regularly spurned, turned to scotch

indicators.note: letters rejected at a steady interval are thrown out, so every other one is kept

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters, with the others discarded

explanation.surface: Rejected time and again, someone took to the whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spurned' looks like the fodder; it is half of the selection signal, and the fodder is the two words after it.
explanation.definitionFit: To scotch a plan is to put an end to it, which is to undo or wreck it.

clue.text: Disheartened, docile wimps returned drunk

indicators.note: losing its heart means the word keeps only its outer letters, with the middle gone
returned means sent back, so the pair is read from the end

blocks.note: docile without its middle letters
wets are feeble, ineffectual people

explanation.surface: Gloomy, meek weaklings came home the worse for drink.
explanation.walkthrough: A wet is British slang for a weak, spineless person.
explanation.definitionFit: Stewed is British slang for heavily intoxicated, one of many informal words for drunk.

clue.text: Shy setter's son lying about character

indicators.note: lying flat and turned about, the whole string is laid down the other way round

blocks.note: to shy is to throw, as is to lob
the setter refers to themself, so the setter's is my
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A bashful crossword compiler's boy fibbing about someone's personality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shy' reads as timid; it is the verb meaning throw, as at a coconut shy.
explanation.definitionFit: A character is a printed letter or sign, and a symbol is a mark of the same kind.
